newsitem.title: MEXICO: Improving Central American economies fuel debt issues.
newsitem.headline: Improving Central American economies fuel debt issues.

text.p: Shrugging off years of internal strife, Central American nations are joining the ranks of their more-developed Latin neighbours by placing bonds in capital markets for receptive investors.
Improving economies, the ongoing peace processes in many of countries and demand for more exotic bonds are all fuelling the debt issues, analysts say.
The debt-issuing countries can benefit by replacing higher cost debt and setting benchmarks for other local debt issuers.
Panama placed a $500 million bond issue earlier this year that was oversubscribed several times.

Guatemala, El Salvador and Costa Rica all plan to go to credit markets this year. Only the region's two poorest countries, Nicaragua and Honduras, have yet to announce any plans, but Honduras is thinking about a bond issue.

"Central American bonds give traditional Latin American investors some exotic flavor and a diversification play rather than the more traditional countries like Argentina and Mexico," said Bankers Trust Research economist Carl W. Ross.
Ironically, the political and civil turmoil in Central America in the 1980s that kept them from borrowing heavily, may actually now help these states reach the capital markets.

"The good news is that these countries were not involved in the syndicated loan markets, so their debt levels are not high relative to South American countries. Their credit stories are very good," said Ignacio Sosa, managing director of emerging markets sales, trading and research for BankBoston.
While many of the larger investment banks may have ignored these countries in the past, that is now changing.
Rating agencies are also assessing quality, although these nations are clearly not yet investment grade.
"There is definitely an improving trend in the region," said Lacey Gallagher, director of sovereign ratings at Standard & Poor's Corp.
Analysts said it will be important for these nations to put the proceeds of their bond issues to good use.
Moreover, added Bankers Trust Research's Ross, "I think that these countries have to be careful not to issue too much debt relative to the size of their economies."
A good example of the swing in sentiment was the Republic of Panama, which placed a $500 million inaugural Eurobond in February. That bond was oversubscribed about three times over.

The five-year bond was doubled in size after an extensive roadshow, with about 70 percent of the paper being bought by U.S. investors. It was the first issue by Panama since 1980 and was used to retire outstanding Brady bonds and to set a benchmark for future corporate issues.

The issue was priced at 175 basis points over similar U.S. Treasuries, a tight level compared with other Latin American borrowers such as Argentina and Mexico. BankBoston led the issue and had previously worked with Panama on a Brady Bond restructuring.
The government has said it has no plans to go to the international capital markets again soon.

Guatemala's planned $150 million issue will be the first in international capital markets for a country that has only recently ended a decades-long war with left-wing guerrillas. After receiving 19 initial proposals to lead its inaugural bond issue, the Guatemalan government narrowed it down to five potential banks before chosing BankBoston.
The roadshow is expected to swing through Asia, Europe and the United States. The debt will be sold in late May or in June, Finance Minister Jose Alejandro Arevalo said recently.

In early May, El Salvador central bank President Roberto Orellana said the country would issue $200 million in seven-year bonds to refinance short-term debt to the International Monetary Fund. The bonds will be used to refinance $150 million of one-year Salvadoran Treasury notes, known as LETES, issued in 1996 through the IMF.
Costa Rica, spared the political turmoil that hit most of its neighbours, said recently it will issue $200 million worth of bonds in September.
"In September, we will place on sale the first $200 million that will help us solve our serious internal debt problem," Information Minister Alejandro Soto told reporters.
The issue will form part of the $500 million that Costa Rica plans to place to help it cut its debt servicing charges. The other $300 million should be placed in the first six months of 1998.
Last December, Costa Rica's outstanding internal debt was calculated at $3.5 billion.

Asked if Honduras had any plans to place a bond, the co-ordinator of external debt with the Finance Ministry, Marcos Carias, told Reuters, "In the short term, we don't have anything planned, but we do think that next year we could use this as an option to manage the government's debt.:
Honduras has external public debt of $3.811 billion, he said.
Nicaragua, which still receives large amounts of international aid, has not yet announced any plans to issue bonds in international capital markets.
